conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal-mental-health clinician. I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with new motherhood, and I’m really glad you’re here.

To help us both get a clear picture of how you’ve been feeling lately, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often shortened to the EPDS. It’s simply a set of 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and experiences over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting or your strength; it’s just a well-tested tool that helps us know what kind of support might be most helpful for you right now.

Everything you share will stay confidential within your care team, and you can take your time or pause at any point. When we’re finished, we’ll talk about the results together and decide on next steps—whether that’s extra resources, follow-up visits, or simply knowing you’re already doing well.

We’ll go through one question at a time. Just answer in your own words; there are no right or wrong answers.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Some days I can still laugh—like when my little guy makes those silly faces while he’s nursing—but it does feel a little forced. It’s not as easy as it used to be, and I catch myself thinking, “I should be enjoying this more.” So, yeah, I’d say it’s been a bit difficult, especially when I’m tired.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can still laugh sometimes—like when the baby does something goofy—but it doesn’t come as naturally as it used to. I have to remind myself to lighten up, and even then it feels kind of flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having coffee with my neighbor—but the excitement isn’t as strong as before. It’s more like “I guess that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the hours.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a few times a week. The other day he spit up a ton right after I laid him down, and I immediately thought, “I must’ve waited too long to burp him—why didn’t I know better?” Even when my partner says it’s normal baby stuff, I still feel like I should’ve prevented it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get little waves of worry, like when he’s napping longer than usual I’ll suddenly think, “Is he still breathing?” It only lasts a minute or two and I can usually talk myself down, but it pops up out of nowhere a couple of times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick jolt of “what-if” when I check the monitor and can’t see his chest rise. My heart races for a few seconds, but I haven’t had a full-blown panic or anything.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When he’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up and I can’t even get a shower, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I usually get through it once he settles, but in the moment it feels overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, it’s not sadness keeping me awake—mostly just my mind replaying the day or listening for every squeak from the crib. Once I doze off I’m out, but it can take me a while to get there.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel kind of down a few days a week—like a gray cloud that comes and goes. It’s not constant, and I still smile at the baby, but I catch myself tearing up over small stuff or just feeling blah.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, I’ve teared up maybe twice this week—once when the bottle leaked all over the couch and once when my mom left after visiting. It wasn’t sobbing, just a quick cry that stopped once I blew my nose.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I want to be here for my baby; I just wish I didn’t feel so off some days.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report with clinician follow-up; 6 wks post-delivery, first baby.

Symptoms / Behaviors endorsed:
- Diminished pleasure / emotional brightness (“laugh feels flat,” excitement “not as strong”)
- Intermittent low mood, tearfulness 2–3×/week, mood lability
- Unwarranted self-blame/guilt several times per week
- Recurrent intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety, brief heart-racing, no full panic attacks
- Episodic feeling of being overwhelmed/drowning when multiple demands coincide
- Initial insomnia related to hyper-vigilance to infant sounds; once asleep, stays asleep

Areas of screening significance:
- Meets sub-threshold for anhedonia and depressed mood
- Mild anxiety symptoms without avoidance or functional impairment
- No self-harm ideation, no suicidal thoughts; protective factor = strong attachment to infant

Risk factors present:
- Partial loss of pleasure, mood reactivity, tearfulness
- Sleep disruption linked to hyper-arousal rather than pure mood
- Self-criticism/guilt exceeding situational basis
- No current safety concerns (explicit denial self-harm)

Screening observation:
Patient exhibits mild to moderate postpartum affective distress characterized by intermittent low mood, reduced enjoyment, and situational anxiety without impairment in basic functioning or infant care. Denies suicidal ideation/intent. Findings suggest consideration for further evaluation for postpartum depression and/or anxiety, and psycho-education/support options.
